Subsets II (input has duplicates)

Sort, then skip a value equal to the previous one at the same level of the recursion (i > start), while still allowing it deeper down. This one line is the standard dedup trick for every "II" variant. O(n · 2ⁿ).
Combination Sum II (each number used once, input has duplicates)
Differs from Combination Sum in two places: recurse with i + 1 (no reuse) and skip equal neighbours. Sorting also lets you break as soon as a candidate exceeds the remainder.
Permutations II (input has duplicates)
Equal values may only be picked left to right, so the second "1" is used only after the first. That removes duplicate orderings without a HashSet of results. O(n · n!).
Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
One recursion level per digit, one branch per letter. O(4ⁿ · n). Using a single StringBuilder and undoing the append is cheaper than creating new strings at every level.
Word Search (does the word exist in the grid?)
Grid DFS with in-place marking that is undone on the way back, so each path cannot reuse a cell. O(R·C·3^L) where L is the word length. For many words at once, see Word Search II with a trie.
Palindrome Partitioning
Choose where the next cut goes, recursing only when the prefix is a palindrome. O(n · 2ⁿ) worst case. A precomputed boolean[][] pal DP table makes each check O(1).
Sudoku Solver

Fill the first empty cell with each valid digit and recurse; a dead end returns false and the caller undoes its choice. The box index trick 3*(r/3) + i/3, 3*(c/3) + i%3 visits the 9 cells of the box. Speed-ups: bitmasks per row/column/box and choosing the cell with the fewest options first.
Subsets vs combinations vs permutations: what changes in the template?

| Subsets | Combinations (size k / target sum) | Permutations
Loop starts at | start | start (or i again if reuse is allowed) | 0, skip used[i]
Record the path | At every call | Only when size == k or sum == target | Only when path.size() == n
Order matters? | No | No | Yes
Number of results | 2ⁿ | C(n, k) | n!
Extra state | start index | start index, remaining sum | boolean[] used
Rule of thumb: order does not matter → pass a start index so you never look back. Order matters → loop from 0 and track used elements.
Handling duplicates: sort + skip vs a HashSet of results

| Sort, then skip equal siblings | Generate all, dedupe with Set<List>
Work done | Never builds a duplicate branch | Builds every duplicate, then throws it away
Extra memory | None beyond the output | A set of all results
Skip rule (subsets / combinations) | if (i > start && a[i] == a[i-1]) continue; | N/A
Skip rule (permutations) | if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1] && !used[i-1]) continue; | N/A
Interview reception | Expected | Accepted only as a first draft
Interview tip: the condition is i > start, not i > 0, for subsets: equal values may appear at different depths, just not as siblings at the same depth.
Mutate and undo vs copy the path at every call

| One shared list, add / remove (backtrack) | New list per call (path + x)
Allocations | Only when saving a result | One copy per call
Bug risk | Forgetting to undo; adding the live list instead of a copy | Low
Extra cost | O(1) per step | O(path length) per step
Strings | StringBuilder: append, then setLength(len) | s + c creates a new String (fine for short paths)
Rule of thumb: use the shared list and always save new ArrayList<>(path). Adding path itself stores a reference that later becomes empty.
Backtracking vs dynamic programming: how do you tell which one a problem needs?

| Backtracking | Dynamic programming
Question asks for | All solutions (list every subset / path / board) | A count, min, max or yes/no
Subproblems repeat? | Not usefully: each path is different | Yes: same (index, remaining) state is reached many ways
Time | Exponential, reduced by pruning | Number of states × work per state
Example pair | Combination Sum (list them) | Coin Change II (count them)
Example pair | Word Break II (all sentences) | Word Break (is it possible?)
Rule of thumb: "return all" → backtracking, because the output itself is exponential. "How many / best" → look for repeated states and memoise them.
